I’ve spent the better part of thirty (30) years dealing with FAA aircraft certification. The 737-MAX 800 crashes were wholly expected by those of us in industry (not specifically, but representative of the problem), and they have nothing to do with derivative certifications and everything to do with lack of independent oversight.

Since the creation of the FAA in the aftermath of the Grand Canyon mid-air collision of 1956, the focus has been on ensuring aviation safety via independent oversight. I don’t have the entire history in front of me, but suffice it to say that for the bulk of my career (starting in 1990), all aircraft certifications were required to be approved by multiple Designated Airworthiness Representatives (DARs) and Designated Engineering Representatives (DERs) who were involved in the development of the aircraft from start to finish. They also were beholden to the FAA and, as such, were completely independent of the aircraft manufacturer. They had ultimate authority on whether any aircraft - new or old - was allowed to fly. Given personalities and subjective biases, it wasn’t a perfect system, but it favored safety over profit.

In 2006, the FAA issued order 8100.15 which created the ability for aircraft manufacturers to function as an Organization Designation Authority (ODA). The simple description is that the manufacturers were given levels of oversight over the certification over their products, rather than having to receive approval exclusively from DARs and DERs. The inmates were now running the asylum. It was only a matter of time before someone died.

When I read the first descriptions of the system that was taking down the 737-MAX aircraft, I was shocked that it had ever been approved. From what I understand to date (ongoing investigation that I’m not privy to, so my understanding is likely flawed or - at best - incomplete, although a close friend of mine has testified before the FAA about it and was quoted in Bloomberg), the system design was as follows:

  1. An aerodynamic stabilization system called MCAS (Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System) was designed to deal with the thrust of the engines as positioned well forward of the wing center. This type of system isn’t novel and similar systems are present in other aircraft; however, it is part of the overall aerodynamics package and is thus a safety critical component. “Safety critical” means, as it sounds, something that is critical to the safety of the aircraft; it’s something that can cause the aircraft to crash if something goes wrong, so extreme measures are taken to ensure that can’t happen.
  2. MCAS has the ability to take control of the aircraft away from the pilot. Again, not unusual and it can be overridden by the pilot, but this makes it even more safety critical.
  3. MCAS is activated by sensor(s) - the optional plural will become important later - that understand the position of the aircraft relative to the airstream it’s flying through in order to prevent the wings from going into a stall condition (lack of lift - i.e., it will start falling from the sky). Stall conditions are more likely to happen during takeoff with the engines further forward on the wings. If it receives information from the sensor(s) indicating a problem, it tries to correct that issue ahead of the pilot.
  4. Anything safety critical goes through extensive safety analysis and gets high levels of scrutiny by safety engineers. There are myriad processes that need to be adhered to. While not necessarily required in all cases, it’s very common to have multiple redundancies on safety critical systems. Kind of like having four brakes on your car as well as an independent braking system between front and rear. This redundant system allows for single failures without complete loss of braking. In the event of a failure, you end up with degraded brakes rather than no brakes at all. Not the best situation, but better than the alternative.
  5. MCAS should have had mandatory, redundant sensors. It didn’t. It had two. As I understand it, two sensors are the minimum required for it to function properly.
  6. MCAS should have warned the pilots of a sensor failure, which would have - at best - grounded the aircraft until they were repaired and - at worst - notified the pilots while in the air that the system was unreliable. Boeing made the sensor failure notification an optional, paid upgrade to the aircraft. WTF?
  7. MCAS could engage multiple times in a short period of time, even when repeatedly overridden by the pilots, and a flaw in the system itself caused each engagement to be more severe than the previous engagement. Imagine Aunt Bee driving a stick shift for the first time - same thing.
  8. The airlines weren’t given training on the system by Boeing.
  9. Boeing was aware of problems in the system and didn’t notify the airlines nor the FAA.

Given the items above, an FAA-beholden DAR/DER team would never have allowed this aircraft into production until the problems with MCAS were addressed to their satisfaction. An ODA, on the other hand, is under control of the manufacturer. This failure is exactly like the Challenger disaster. Management, concerned about pressures of various types (political pressure in the case of NASA, monetary pressure in the case of Boeing), had no one above them to tell them, “No!” There is no doubt in my mind that this disaster was bound to happen. The biggest surprise to me is that it took this long.
